Current project, project details

Empowering construction workforce resilience in Hong Kong: an AI-driven forecasting platform for workforce planning

Funder
Hong Kong Construction Industry Council, Research and Technology Development Fund (Explorative Project Scheme)
Role
Principal investigator, with co-investigators Albert P.C. Chan and M.W. Chan
Period
From December 2026, 18 months
Based at
The Hong Kong Polytechnic University

Abstract

Hong Kong expects more than HK$120 billion a year in capital works over the next decade, yet the supply of skilled trades still does not match demand on site: some trades stand idle while others run short. Workforce planning still relies on static labour multipliers and broad trade groups, and site labour records are rarely used. This project combines artificial intelligence, which learns deployment patterns from site labour, training and project records, with system dynamics, which shows how training, wages and policy feed back on supply over time. The result is a web-based dashboard that gives monthly, trade-by-trade forecasts, warns of shortages or surpluses ahead, and lets government, contractors, training bodies and workers test what-if scenarios before they act.

The problems it tackles

  • Mismatch by tradeSome trades stand idle while others run short, which delays projects and raises costs.
  • Static forecastsLabour multipliers and broad trade groups miss how demand and supply respond to change.
  • Little visibilityTraining bodies and workers cannot see shortages or job openings coming.

How the platform works

  1. Step 1
    Learn from the records

    Site labour deployment and attendance records from public and private sites, training enrolments and completions, and a database of more than 1,500 completed and ongoing projects.

  2. Step 2
    Forecast with machine learning

    An ensemble of models forecasts monthly demand and supply for each trade, scored for accuracy against past data.

    XGBoostLightGBMSupport vector machinesNeural networksLSTMTemporal Fusion Transformer

  3. Step 3
    Simulate the feedback

    A system dynamics model adds what static forecasts miss: training delays, attrition, wages, project timing and the effect of modular integrated construction.

  4. Step 4
    Plan on the dashboard

    A web dashboard shows shortages and surpluses ahead, the factors behind each forecast, and the result of what-if scenarios, for government, contractors, training bodies, workers and unions.

New data retrains the models regularly, so the forecasts improve as the platform is used.

Eighteen months, three phases

161218
Understand the systemInterviews with 25 to 30 contractors, unions and training bodies; causal-loop maps checked by an expert focus group
Months 1–5
Data and machine learningAssemble the project, labour and training data; train and test the forecasting models
Months 2–12
Integrate, validate and launchJoin AI forecasts to the system dynamics model; expert workshops and back-testing; build the dashboard
Months 11–18

What the project will deliver

  • An open-access web dashboard for government bodies and industry, with trade-by-trade forecasts and scenario tools.
  • Site trials on five active construction sites with main contractors, in the second half of the project.
  • Two journal papers and an international conference presentation.
  • Stakeholder workshops and a closing seminar with a live demonstration for policymakers, contractors, training providers and unions.

Current project, project details

Development of a data-driven prediction model for the condition assessment of ageing residential building stock

Funder
Hong Kong Research Grants Council, General Research Fund
Role
Principal investigator, with co-investigators Joseph H.K. Lai, Albert P.C. Chan and M.W. Chan
Period
From January 2026, 36 months
Based at
Department of Building and Real Estate, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University

Abstract

By the end of 2024, more than 28,000 private residential buildings in Hong Kong had reached 30 years or older, about 64% of the stock. Many have had decades of too little maintenance, and owners often cannot afford inspection and repair. At the current pace of mandatory inspection, one full cycle of the ageing stock would take more than 20 years. This project develops a data-driven prediction model for the condition of ageing residential buildings. A dynamic Bayesian network learns how defects in walls, roofs, drainage and building services lead to one another over time, drawing on real building inspection reports and expert knowledge. A convolutional neural network reads panoramic photographs to detect defects automatically and keeps the model up to date. Owners, surveyors and the building authority can then predict deterioration, rank buildings by urgency and test maintenance strategies before they adopt them.

The problems it tackles

  • A fast-ageing stockAbout 64% of private residential buildings are 30 years or older, and falling concrete and rendering have raised public concern.
  • Inspection cannot keep upAt today’s pace, one inspection cycle of the ageing stock would take more than 20 years.
  • Piecemeal assessmentMost methods rate single components by eye and miss how one defect leads to another.

How the model is built: five stages over 36 months

  1. Stage 1
    Organise the building

    A taxonomy of components, from external walls and roofs to drainage and building services. Key defects and causes are text-mined from at least 500 inspection reports and checked by 10 to 15 experts.

  2. Stage 2
    Map cause and effect

    Structural equation modelling of at least 200 survey responses, then a Delphi panel of 15 or more experts, sets out how defects lead to one another.

  3. Stage 3
    Predict over time

    A dynamic Bayesian network splits deterioration into stages, such as cracks that lead to spalling and façade failure, and rates overall condition from very good to very bad.

    Dynamic Bayesian networkText mining

  4. Stage 4
    See defects automatically

    A convolutional neural network reads panoramic photographs of 200 buildings to detect defects such as debonded tiles and corroded pipes, and feeds them into the network.

    Convolutional neural networkImage recognition

  5. Stage 5
    Validate on real buildings

    Sensitivity tests, then ten recently inspected buildings compared with their official inspection reports, including the time and cost saved against manual inspection.

New inspection reports and photographs keep updating the network, so its predictions improve over time.

Pathway to impact

  1. 1 to 3 yearsFind problems earlyFlag urgent defects, rank buildings for maintenance, and prepare for external-wall risks.
  2. 3 to 5 yearsPlan and budgetForecast how the stock will deteriorate under current policy, and allocate maintenance budgets precisely.
  3. 5 to 10 yearsTarget renewalFocus rehabilitation on the groups of buildings that need it most, and inform redevelopment and urban resilience planning.

What the project will deliver

  • A validated prediction model that assesses and forecasts building condition and updates itself with new inspection and image data.
  • An image-recognition tool that detects defects in panoramic photographs of building exteriors.
  • Open knowledge transfer: findings and algorithms on a public website, and technology transfer through PolyU’s Institute for Entrepreneurship.
  • Journal papers, international conferences and professional seminars with facility management and building surveying institutions.

Current project, project details

Enhancing inclusivity in Hong Kong’s outdoor facilities and venues: a study on ethnic minorities’ access and preferences

Funder
Public Policy Research Funding Scheme, HKSAR Government
Role
Principal investigator, with co-investigators Esther H.K. Yung, Nan Cao and Bryant P.H. Hui
Period
From November 2025, 12 months
Study area
Yau Tsim Mong, the district with Hong Kong’s highest share of ethnic-minority residents

Abstract

In a city of small homes, outdoor facilities and venues, from parks and sports grounds to plazas, are where community life happens. Ethnic minorities are a key part of Hong Kong’s society, yet design barriers and a lack of cultural sensitivity keep many from using these spaces. Recent Policy Addresses and the Hong Kong 2030+ strategy call for inclusive, universal design, but planning guidelines say little about ethnic minorities’ needs. This study combines GIS analysis of where facilities are and how easy they are to reach, questionnaires and field observation with ethnic-minority users, and immersive virtual-reality experiments that measure how people respond to culturally relevant designs. The results rank what matters most to ethnic-minority users and turn it into practical recommendations for inclusive planning and design.

The problems it tackles

  • Space is scarceWith small homes, public outdoor spaces carry much of daily life, from rest and play to meeting friends.
  • Guidelines are generalPlanning standards address older people and people with disabilities, but rarely ethnic minorities’ needs.
  • Barriers beyond provisionLanguage, booking systems and culturally unresponsive design keep people away even where facilities exist.

How the study works: five stages over 12 months

  1. Stage 1
    Frame the questions

    Focus groups with 10 to 15 experts from NGOs and ethnic-minority support services, then a questionnaire for about 270 ethnic-minority residents.

  2. Stage 2
    Map the facilities

    GIS analysis of where facilities are and how easy they are to reach, from land use and street connectivity to homes and transport, plus field observation.

  3. Stage 3
    Test designs in virtual reality

    In an immersive CAVE (Cave Automatic Virtual Environment), participants experience culturally relevant and neutral virtual venues; picture-based scales measure their response without language barriers.

    Immersive VRSelf-Assessment ManikinPerceived Restorativeness Scale

  4. Stage 4
    Model preferences

    An ordered logit model links background, facility attributes and psychological response to show what matters most.

  5. Stage 5
    Validate and recommend

    Focus groups with the groups concerned and a stakeholder workshop test the findings before they become policy recommendations.

Emerging findings

22

30

4,061
interview and survey segments coded

Physical provision alone is not enough. Use depends on language, booking systems, culturally responsive design and awareness, and NGO-led programmes do most to bring people in.

Recommendations taking shape

  • Multilingual booking systems and signage
  • Walk-in access, to reduce reliance on booking
  • Structured partnerships between NGOs and government for community programmes
  • Facility zones that respond to the needs of women and girls

1. AI cash-flow forecasting

Sing, Ma, Chan and Chan, Project Leadership and Society (2026)Read the paper (opens in a new tab)Open access

Infrastructure projects do not spend money the same way: some load spending early, some late, some evenly. Standard models force one pattern on all of them. Our model first describes each project’s own spending path with a path signature, a compact mathematical summary of the path, and feeds it with the raw history into an LSTM network. Tested on 282 completed roads, water treatment, school and hospital projects, it forecasts the next 12 months from the last 24.

  1. Step 1
    Monthly spending

    The last 24 months of a live project’s actual expenditure.

  2. Step 2
    Path signature

    Turns the spending path into features that keep its order, turns and higher-order interactions, so each project keeps its own pattern.

  3. Step 3
    LSTM network

    A recurrent neural network learns from the signature features and the raw history together.

  4. Step 4
    12-month forecast

    Next year’s spending, the horizon used for annual budgets, so leaders see drift early.

The forecasts feed budgeting and early warnings, so project leaders can act before spending drifts.

Why it matters

  • One model for different projects. It handles front-loaded, back-loaded and balanced spending without splitting projects into groups.
  • Deeper signatures, better forecasts. Accuracy rose as the signature captured more of each path’s structure (R² from 0.876 to 0.896).
  • Built for governance. A 12-month view matches annual budgeting, liquidity planning and portfolio oversight.

2. Four more ways the team uses AI

Neural networks set contingency from project complexity

Seven machine-learning models were trained on 122 completed public infrastructure projects in Hong Kong to predict how much cost contingency a project will really use. A neural network was the most accurate. Adding a complexity index, built from project size and duration, raised its R² from 0.808 to 0.889 and cut its average error by 27%.

Bootstrapping and Monte Carlo dropout turn the single figure into a range. With the index, 88% of actual outcomes fell inside the bootstrapped range, up from 80%.

Sing, Ma and Gu, Applied Sciences (2025)Read the paper (opens in a new tab)Open access

Outside view meets inside view for contingency

Across 33 completed projects worth over HK$36 billion, reference class forecasting at P70 and P80 was more accurate overall, while project-by-project risk analysis did better for drainage works. The paper sets out how to combine the two, and where machine learning can keep contingencies up to date.

Reference class forecastingProbabilistic risk analysisWilcoxon test

Sing, Kazeem, Chan and Liu, Production Planning & Control (2026)Read the paper (opens in a new tab)Open access

Deep learning reads risk registers

BERTopic, a transformer-based topic model, read 1,503 risk descriptions from 277 public works projects and found 11 cost risk factors, from design changes and market conditions to project delay and underground conditions. Its topics were more coherent than those of LDA, NMF, CTM, Top2Vec and GPT-4.1.

Sentence embeddingsUMAPHDBSCAN clusteringc-TF-IDF topics

Machine learning forecasts the maintenance workforce

Four models were trained on 128 records of seven indicators from maintenance contractors. XGBoost was the most accurate, with R² of 0.99 on test data against 0.88 for a neural network, and an LSTM network forecast the value of maintenance work that drives labour demand.

Research

AI for infrastructure, buildings and cities

My research has two areas: making infrastructure delivery predictable, and keeping ageing buildings and cities resilient. In both, I use AI and machine learning to predict cost, risk, workforce needs and building condition, and turn the results into tools that agencies use to plan, budget and maintain. Most of the questions come from government and industry.

Four topics: select a card to explore each one.

How the research works

AI and machine learning for infrastructure management

The same four steps run through both research areas. Models learn from records the industry already keeps, are tested under uncertainty, and end as tools that agencies and asset owners can use.

  1. Learn from the records

    Risk registers, cash-flow and payment records, inspection reports, workforce data and street-level images.

  2. Machine learning and AI

    Neural networks, deep learning and LSTM forecasting, large language models and agentic AI.

  3. Test under uncertainty

    Probabilistic risk analysis, Monte Carlo and system dynamics simulation, and reference class forecasting.

  4. Support the decision

    Contingency estimates, cash-flow early warnings, workforce plans and maintenance priorities.

Research area 1

Infrastructure performance, risk and delivery

Cost and schedule performance, contingency, workforce capacity, safety, rework and megaproject benchmarking. My recent work shows that reference class forecasting and probabilistic risk analysis are complementary rather than competing, and sets out how to use them together in public-works estimates.

How a city’s building stock ages, and what policy can change

Stock-and-flow models follow buildings as they age, decay and are rehabilitated, so inspection and subsidy policies can be tested over decades before they are adopted. The same approach models the workforce infrastructure programmes need.

Retrofitting simulation for public housing estates

Groups ageing residential blocks into clusters of similar buildings, then uses BIM and energy simulation to compare retrofit packages across each cluster, so investment goes to the options that save the most.

Government & industry

Work with government and industry

I spent eight years in the surveying discipline of the Hong Kong Government, and much of my research is still commissioned by public bodies. Each project follows the same five steps, from a real problem to a tool the client uses.

  1. 1

    A real problem

    An agency or industry body brings a cost, workforce or asset question.

  2. 2

    A research question

    Framed so the answer can be tested against data.

  3. 3

    Analytical modelling

    Probabilistic, machine-learning or simulation models.

  4. 4

    A validated tool

    Checked against past projects before anyone relies on it.

  5. 5

    Adopted in practice

    Built into the client’s own procedures and systems.

Government commission, project details

Evidence-based contingency for Hong Kong’s public works

Client
Development Bureau, HKSAR Government
Study
Review and enhancement of Estimating Using Risk Analysis (ERA)
Role
Lead Consultant and Project Manager
Period
2018, with a further phase from 2024 to 2025

Hong Kong’s public works set contingency through Estimating Using Risk Analysis. I helped the Bureau add a probabilistic layer to it: probability curves fitted to past project records, a Monte Carlo engine, and calibration against how completed projects turned out, so contingency is estimated consistently and backed by evidence.

How the model works

  1. 1
    Collect the evidence

    Risk registers and cost records from past public works projects, across project types and contract forms.

    Past project records
  2. 2
    Fit probability curves

    Each risk factor, from client changes to uncharted utilities, gets its best-fit distribution for each project type.

    Best-fit distributions
  3. 3
    Simulate

    Monte Carlo runs combine the risks into a full range of outcomes, giving contingency at P50, P80, P90 and P95.

    Thousands of runs per project
  4. 4
    Calibrate and deploy

    Results checked against completed-project outcomes, then built into a web-based tool for project officers.

    Web-based tool

What the Bureau received

  • A web-based Monte Carlo tool. Officers enter a project, adjust pre-loaded risks and read off contingency at each confidence level.
  • Guidance and training. A step-by-step procedure and user guide so project teams apply the method consistently.
  • Evidence for budget confidence levels. Advice on balancing the risk of overrun against tying up capital in over-cautious reserves.

Government commission, project details

Cash-flow early warning for Hong Kong’s capital works

Client
Development Bureau, HKSAR Government
Studies
Upgrading, review and maintenance of the Project Surveillance System, with reference class forecasting for cost and schedule
Role
Consultant
Period
2023 to 2025

The Project Surveillance System compares each capital project’s spending with the patterns of completed projects and flags those drifting off course, so senior management can step in early. I helped the Bureau strengthen it: benchmark curves from projects that finished on time and on budget, monitoring through to the final account, support for an AI forecasting application, and refreshed reference classes for cost and schedule.

How the early warning works

  1. 1
    Learn from past projects

    Cash-flow records from completed capital projects, checked, cleaned and grouped by project type.

    Completed-project records
  2. 2
    Put projects on one timeline

    Each project’s spending is rescaled to ten equal stages, so projects of any length can be compared.

    Standard S-curves
  3. 3
    Set the performance zones

    Projects that finished on time and on budget define green, yellow and red zones around the expected curve.

    Green, yellow, red zones
  4. 4
    Warn early

    Live projects are tracked against the zones, and alerts show which ones need attention, and when.

    Earlier alerts

What the Bureau received

  • Stricter benchmark curves. Built from well-performing projects, they flagged drifting projects earlier when tested on recently completed work.
  • Monitoring to the final account. The curves now run past completion, so spending is followed until the accounts close.
  • An AI forecasting application. Support for developing and testing a web application that forecasts cost and schedule performance.
  • Refreshed reference classes. Updated cost uplift curves and new schedule curves, read as in the chart above, so allowances match the certainty a project needs.

Professional body commission, project details

Evidence for a professional guide to inspecting post-1980 buildings

Client
Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, Building Surveying Division
Study
Research for the Professional Guide to Building Inspection, Volume 2: Post-1980 Residential and Composite Buildings in Hong Kong
Role
Lead Academic Consultant
Period
Survey 2022; research report 2023; findings published in Facilities (2026)

Hong Kong’s post-1980 residential and composite buildings are entering the age when inspection and repair become routine, yet practice varies. The study gave the Institute research-based evidence on how building surveyors inspect these buildings, which defects matter most and where practitioners need support, to shape its professional guide.

How the study worked

  1. 1
    Review and pilot

    A literature review set the topics, and experienced building surveyors tested the questionnaire before launch.

    Piloted questionnaire
  2. 2
    Survey the profession

    An online survey of the Institute’s building surveyors on inspection practice, defects and new techniques, analysed statistically.

    Practitioner survey
  3. 3
    Test with practitioners

    A focus group of experienced surveyors checked the results, settled contradictions and shared best practice.

    Focus group
  4. 4
    Recommend

    Recommendations on what the guide should cover, from defect causes to report templates and inspection techniques.

    Guide recommendations

What the study found

  • Monitoring and pathology are the hardest part of an inspection, and report writing takes the most time.
  • Water seepage, concrete cracks and curtain walls need the closest attention. Visual inspection is the usual method, but it is less reliable at height and in lightwells.
  • Blockages and misconnections are the most common drainage defects, above and below ground.
  • Early involvement of maintenance professionals in design is the surest way to make buildings easier to maintain.
  • Drones, laser scanning and computer-aided surveys are known to surveyors, but their use in Hong Kong is still at an early stage.

What the Institute received

  • A research report ranking the symptoms, causes and inspection methods for each defect type, checked by practitioners.
  • Recommendations for the guide: defect causes, a report template, and techniques that make inspection more reliable and efficient.

Also on this card: workforce planning for the Construction Industry Council

From 2009 to 2012 I worked on the Council’s manpower research for the construction industry, workforce projection updates, technician projections and a study of workforce mobility. The labour-multiplier and stock-flow models from that work still underpin its industry-wide workforce forecasts. In 2017, as lead consultant, I drafted the Council’s reference materials on the selection of contractors.

How the AI tutor works

1Designed by the teacher

  • Curated knowledge baseCourse materials and the two assigned journal papers, so answers stay within the subject.
  • Task promptsExplain in simple language, give examples and encourage follow-up questions.
  • A learning pathA node-based workflow, built like an activity-on-node network.

2The tutor, open 24/7

Illustrative exchange

When should a client choose design-and-build rather than traditional procurement?

When the client wants one point of responsibility and an earlier start, and can accept less control over the design. For your case, which matters most: time, cost certainty or design quality?

The learning path, drawn as an activity-on-node network

  1. Choose a topic or paper
  2. Read a section
  3. Ask and follow up
  4. Back to the main path

Built on Botpress. Students treat answers as a guide to check, not an authority.

3Evidence back to the teacher

  • Interaction recordsStudents hand in their tutor transcripts with the assignment and a quiz.
  • Thinking-level analysisQuestions coded by Bloom’s level with AI help, then checked by hand.
  • 53% asked follow-up questionsStudents probed further on the research papers, rather than stopping at the first answer.

The records show where students struggle, so the next class and the tutor’s support can be aimed there. The teacher keeps the design, guidance and assessment.

How a week runs

  1. 1
    Before class

    AI-guided reading, concept checks and quizzes, so students arrive knowing what they find difficult.

    1,628 messages from 58 students
  2. 2
    In class

    Contact time goes to network analysis, critical path calculations, planning cases and procurement exercises.

    Class time for problem-solving
  3. 3
    After class

    Review, reflection and assignment preparation at each student’s own pace.

    6,094 messages from 52 students

The research-paper assignment. Students worked through two journal papers on path float and precedence networks with the tutor, then handed in their transcripts and sat a quiz. 11,109 messages from 164 students; average mark 85.9 out of 100.

About

A surveyor first, then an academic

I am a chartered building surveyor, born and educated in Hong Kong. I spent my first eight years in the Hong Kong Government, in the surveying discipline of the Buildings Department and the Architectural Services Department, and the work went well beyond inspection. It taught me that good decisions balance technical limits, regulation, budgets and people, and it still shapes what I research and how I teach.

Eight years in government, across the life of a building

  1. PlanNew development schemesPlan scrutiny and statutory building control
  2. DeliverProject managementMaintenance and alteration works
  3. RegulateBuilding control and enforcementStatutory control of existing buildings
  4. DiagnoseCondition surveysCondition assessment and defect diagnosis

The same span runs through my research, from project delivery to the ageing building stock.

Since 2012 I’ve worked full time in universities in Australia and Hong Kong. I took my PhD at Curtin University in Perth, stayed on as Senior Lecturer, and later spent four years as Associate Professor at the University of Newcastle, where I led the Master of Project Management through accreditation by the Australian Institute of Project Management. I’m now at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, and I keep close ties with Australia as an Adjunct Professor at the University of Canberra and an assessor for the Australian Research Council.

Professional qualifications in the UK, Hong Kong and Australia

  • UK and worldwideFRICSFellow, Royal Institution of Chartered SurveyorsChartered Building Surveyor and Property and Facilities Management Surveyor. Member from 2013, Fellow from 2023.
  • Hong KongMHKISMember, Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors
  • AustraliaMAIBSMember, Australian Institute of Building Surveyors
  • AustraliaMAIPMMember, Australian Institute of Project Management

I also assess other surveyors. Chairperson of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ Assessment of Professional Competence Panel since 2023, with more than 20 assessments chaired in Hong Kong and Australia. I have also led degrees through accreditation by the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, the Australian Institute of Building and the Australian Institute of Project Management.

Quick facts

Disciplines
Building surveying; construction and project management; infrastructure and built-asset management; property and facilities management; real estate and the built environment.
Research areas
Infrastructure cost risk and contingency, construction workforce forecasting, megaproject performance, the condition and maintenance of ageing buildings, and urban resilience. Methods include AI and machine learning, probabilistic modelling and simulation.
Leadership
Programme Leader of the BSc (Hons) in Surveying at PolyU, with more than 300 students; before that, Deputy Programme Leader of the Doctor of International Real Estate and Construction (DIREC). Previously Program Convenor (Program Director) of the Master of Project Management and the Graduate Diploma in Project Management, and a School Executive member at the University of Newcastle. Lead consultant and project manager on studies for the Development Bureau, the Construction Industry Council and the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors. Founding Secretary of the Centre for Infrastructure Delivery, Associate Editor of Built Environment Project and Asset Management, editor of an Edward Elgar research companion, and Chairperson of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ Assessment of Professional Competence (APC) Panel.
Teaching
Construction law and contract administration, development control, project management and procurement, project planning and cost planning with BIM, building surveying, building maintenance and asset management, and research methods. From first year to professional doctorate, face to face and online.
Professional standing
Fellow of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (FRICS) since 2023, and a member since 2013; Member of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors (MHKIS), Member of the Australian Institute of Building Surveyors (MAIBS) and Member of the Australian Institute of Project Management (MAIPM). Chairperson of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors’ Assessment of Professional Competence (APC) Panel. Led degrees through accreditation by the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors and the Australian Institute of Building at Curtin University, and by the Australian Institute of Project Management at the University of Newcastle.
Professional ethics
Bound by the Rules of Conduct of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors. Chairperson of its Assessment of Professional Competence Panel since 2023, with more than 20 assessments chaired in Hong Kong and Australia that test candidates’ competence, ethics and statutory knowledge. Formerly a member of Curtin University’s Human Research Ethics Committee, and co-author of five recent papers on integrity-based ethics management in construction.
Doctoral supervision
Six PhD candidates supervised to completion, plus two professional doctorates. Chief supervisor of three current PhD candidates at PolyU and co-supervisor of one at the University of Canberra. Thesis examiner for RMIT University, the University of Technology Sydney and Western Sydney University.
Collaboration
Open to joint research, industry partnerships, advisory and consultancy work, PhD supervision and examining, and visiting, adjunct and leadership appointments, with universities, government and research organisations in Hong Kong, the UK and Australia.
